card.name: Fa’ataupati
card.tagline: The rhythmic Samoan slap dance mimicking the swatting of mosquitoes.
card.profile: The Fa’ataupati is a vigorous Samoan men's dance characterized by synchronized body percussion. Performed without external instruments, the dancers use their own bodies as drums through forceful slapping of the chest, thighs, and arms. It is the only all-male dance in Samoa and requires significant physical strength and stability. Traditionally, dancers apply heavy amounts of coconut oil to protect the skin from the intensity of the rhythmic strikes.
card.insight: The dance originated in the 19th century as a rhythmic response to a mosquito invasion, turning the act of slapping insects off the skin into a percussive art form.
card.profile_long:
The Fa’ataupati stands as a unique percussive tradition within the Samoan archipelago, distinguished by its lack of external musical accompaniment. Developed in the 19th century, the dance is a physical manifestation of everyday survival; it is said to have been born from the arrival of mosquito swarms in the Kingdom. The word 'pati' translates to 'clap,' while 'Fa’ataupati' refers to the act of forcefully clapping or slapping. What began as the practical, frantic movement of swatting biting insects was eventually codified into a disciplined, synchronized performance of strength and coordination. 

In performance, the Fa’ataupati is an exhibition of male vitality. Dancers perform in groups, as the dance is rarely seen as a solo endeavor. The music is generated entirely by the performers' bodies: the sharp crack of palms against the chest, the duller thud of slaps on the thighs, and the rhythmic stomping of feet against the ground. Because the slapping is forceful enough to leave physical marks, performers traditionally coat their bodies in coconut oil to provide a protective layer and a characteristic sheen. 

While rooted in 19th-century history, the Fa’ataupati remains a vital part of Samoan cultural identity and has influenced modern performance art. It has transitioned from village squares to international stages, notably being integrated into the repertoire of contemporary dance companies like Black Grace in New Zealand. Despite these modern adaptations, the core of the dance remains unchanged—a high-energy, percussive display that requires the dancers to move in perfect unison, maintaining a steady tempo through physical impact alone.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance was developed in Samoa during the 19th century. It is historically linked to an invasion of mosquitoes in the Kingdom, where the repetitive motions of slapping insects off the body were transformed into a rhythmic dance.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers perform in a group, maintaining synchronicity while slapping various parts of their bodies including the chest and thighs. The dance requires strength, stability, and the use of coconut oil on the skin to prevent bruising from the forceful impacts.
sections.music_and_instruments: This is the only Samoan dance that requires no external instruments. The music is created solely through body percussion: slapping the body, clapping hands, and stomping feet.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers typically perform with bare torsos heavily rubbed with coconut oil. The setting is traditionally communal, though it is now performed on stages globally.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance mimics the everyday activity of swatting mosquitoes, representing a cultural adaptation of a historical nuisance into a display of male strength and coordination.
sections.notable_figures: The New Zealand contemporary dance company Black Grace is noted for incorporating Fa’ataupati into their works 'Minoi' and 'Minoi 2'.
sections.lineage: The dance is indigenous to Samoans and is classified as the only all-male dance in the culture.

basic_steps: Apply coconut oil to the chest, arms, and legs
Stand in a group formation with a stable, wide stance
Slap the chest with open palms in sync with the group
Stomp feet to provide a bass rhythm
teaching.rhythm: Percussive and synchronized, generated by body slaps and stomps
teaching.level_notes: Requires high physical endurance and the ability to maintain tempo without melodic accompaniment.

claims.text: The dance was developed in Samoa in the 19th century and is only performed by males.
The name Fa’ataupati means to forcefully clap or to slap.
The dance mimics a person slapping mosquitoes off their body.
It is the only Samoan dance that uses no instruments, relying on body percussion.
Dancers use coconut oil to protect their skin from the slapping.

lessons.title: Samoan Slap Dance Tutorial
lessons.counting_scheme: 1-2-3-4 / lualua tongi e / a'a tongi e

parts.note: Teacher introduces the Samoan slap dance (Fa'ataupati).
First step breakdown with jumps and stomps.
Second step breakdown hitting legs and chest.

steps.name: First Step (Lualua tongi e)
steps.counts: lualua tongi e / e a'a tongi e
steps.description: Stomp and clap combo while jumping right and left.

steps.name: Second Step
steps.description: Jump and hit legs, chest, sides, and swing down.

safety: Make sure your in a good stance like your on a horse
Keep your back straight and bent down
lessons.teacher_style: The teacher explains steps methodically with verbal counts and repetition. He breaks down combinations slowly and drills them multiple times before connecting them.
lessons.distinctive_method: Integrating traditional Samoan vocal cues and call-and-response phrases directly into the physical drills.
what_works: Repeating sequences multiple times before moving on
what_hinders: Fast transitions between detailed explanations and full speed demonstrations

evidence.observation: Teacher demonstrates squat stance with straight back and hands on hips, turning to the side to show posture.
Teacher performs stomping and clapping sequence while facing front.

observation.setting: A spacious wooden-floored hall or studio with large windows and red hanging lamps, with a few people seated watching.
observation.dancers: A group of around 11 men, shirtless, dancing together.
observation.formation_and_space: A horizontal line facing forward, occasionally shifting positions or making circular/line movements across the floor.
observation.posture: Torsos upright or slightly leaning forward, knees bent in a wide stance, weight shifted dynamically between feet.
observation.footwork: Stomping and stepping vigorously on the beat, keeping knees bent and lifting feet with heel or whole-foot contact.
observation.arms_and_hands: Arms swing, clap sharply against hands and body, or extend outward with fists clenched or fingers open.
observation.hips_and_torso: Torsos remain mostly upright while moving up and down with knee bounces; some bending forward from the waist.
observation.levels_jumps_turns: Staying low in a knee-bent level with occasional deep bends and sharp jumps or turns.
observation.costume_and_props: Traditional-style red and white wraps around the waist, with straw or textured ankle guards.
observation.cannot_infer: Exact foot placement details and subtle weight transfers cannot be verified due to camera angle and distance.

signature_moments.what: Group stands in a wide squat, knees bent, stomping rhythmically while clapping their hands and slapping their thighs.
Dancers stamp and hop rapidly in place while swinging arms across their bodies in unison.
Dancers shuffle in a circular motion while singing in chorus and tapping their chests or thighs.
Synchronized deep knee dips accompanied by sharp chest slaps and coordinated vocal shouts.
